knot-symmetric.caption: The symmetric (Turkish) knot: the yarn wraps two warps and both ends come up between them. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 1.
knot-symmetric.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

knot-asymmetric.caption: The asymmetric (Persian) knot: the yarn wraps one warp and passes under the next, so one end comes up beside it. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 4.
knot-asymmetric.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

knot-jufti.caption: Jufti knots: knots tied over four warps instead of two.
knot-jufti.credit: Arie M. den Toom, via Wikimedia Commons

kpsi-coarse.caption: One square inch of a rug’s back at 7 knots to the inch each way (49 to the square inch). Each knot shows as two small bumps.

kpsi-medium.caption: One square inch at 10 knots to the inch each way (100 to the square inch).

kpsi-fine.caption: One square inch at 14 knots to the inch each way (196 to the square inch).

kpsi-very-fine.caption: One square inch at 20 knots to the inch each way (400 to the square inch).

warp-wool.caption: Wool warps: the fringe of a rug woven on wool, soft and slightly fuzzy, ivory to tan.
warp-wool.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum Tāmaki Paenga Hira, via Wikimedia Commons

warp-cotton.caption: Cotton warps: a white, smooth, evenly twisted fringe.
warp-cotton.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum Tāmaki Paenga Hira, via Wikimedia Commons

warp-silk.caption: Silk warps: a fine, glossy fringe on a silk rug.

warp-hair.caption: Goat hair: coarse, wiry and dark, here woven into a tent. Goat or camel hair is used for warps and edges in some tribal rugs.
warp-hair.credit: David Stanley from Nanaimo, Canada, via Wikimedia Commons

offset-level.caption: Warps level: both loops of each knot show side by side on the back. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 7a.
offset-level.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

offset-offset.caption: One warp of each knot partly sunk: the back looks slightly ridged. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 8a.
offset-offset.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

offset-depressed.caption: One warp of each knot sunk under the other: only one loop shows, and the back looks ribbed. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 10a.
offset-depressed.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

wefts-1.caption: One weft between each row of knots. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 15.
wefts-1.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

wefts-2.caption: Two wefts between each row of knots. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 16.
wefts-2.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

wefts-3.caption: Three wefts between each row of knots. Hawley, Plate B, fig. 17.
wefts-3.credit: Hawley, Oriental Rugs, Antique and Modern (1913; 1922 printing)

weft-wool.caption: Wool: soft and slightly fuzzy, ivory to tan or dyed.
weft-wool.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum Tāmaki Paenga Hira, via Wikimedia Commons

weft-cotton.caption: The back of a rug on cotton warps and wefts: the white cotton shows between the knots.
weft-cotton.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum Tāmaki Paenga Hira, via Wikimedia Commons

weft-hair.caption: Goat hair: coarse, wiry and dark.
weft-hair.credit: David Stanley from Nanaimo, Canada, via Wikimedia Commons

pile-wool.caption: Wool pile: soft, with a matt or gentle sheen.
pile-wool.credit: Auckland War Memorial Museum Tāmaki Paenga Hira, via Wikimedia Commons

pile-silk.caption: Silk pile: very fine, with a strong sheen that changes with the light.

pile-art-silk.caption: Viscose (rayon), the fiber sold as “art silk”: very shiny and smooth.

pile-hair.caption: Goat hair: coarse, wiry and dark. Camel hair is softer and tan to brown.
pile-hair.credit: David Stanley from Nanaimo, Canada, via Wikimedia Commons
